posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md: Have you tried it? I did and it's not as easy as it sounds. I just sandwich the film between glass with no index matching, but I also get woodgrain. Luckily I just use film for tests and shoot the final piece on glass, so it doesn't the woodgrain doesn't matter. If the final hologram is to be on film, I'd suggest index matching, even though the stuff is horrible, gooey and gets everywhere!

posts.topic_title: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md:
Other people have tried the static lamination and found that it doesn't work well on roll film and that the laminating material is very expensive.

It's cheaper and easier to use Kapco or something similar and permanently laminate the film to glass. Keep your environment clean and it's not hard to keep dust out from between the glass and film.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md:
I'll work up a tutorial (at least the text) while I'm stuck on an airplane and in hotel the next couple of days.

In a nutshell, start at one end and roll out the film using only the roller. Don't let the film touch the laminating material until the roller has forced it down.

The same is true of the laminating material when applying it to glass.

I'll put more details in the tutorial.

posts.topic_title: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md:
> **andy75180:** With my crude attempt at sticking on film last week. I noticed I had to increase the exposure with this film/plate idea.

Actually I've experienced the same effect with the Kapco film. My working theory is that the film base is hydrophylic (absorbs moisture) and allows development to happen from both sides of the emulsion, thereby decreasing the development time. With the film adhered to glass, development only happens from one side. I've just thought about sealing the non-emulsion side of the film with some sort of spray-on sealer and doing some tests but don't have time for that right now. I'll put it on my "some day" list though. Right now, I just work with the results and either increase my exposure or development time slightly.

> **andy75180:** Do you use this idea all the time now instead of buying plates?

I do for all my transmission masters. I sometimes use it for reflections but only when playing around. I prefer to mount the reflection holograms after they're completely processed and I know I've got a keeper. I'm not so good that all my holograms are keepers. 

> **andy75180:** Have you ever tried using the removable adhesive sheets? Roll out film as usual, after exposure just peel of the holographic film?

I never have. I was never able to get a sample of the material that Slavich recommends and I'm not willing to shell out a several hundred $ for something that might not work.

posts.topic_title: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.author: HoloM
posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md:
I use this technique which is explained on the slavich website to temporary laminate the film on glass. This works well, even for film which is of a roll. 

But I use it only for transmission masters and rainbow copies. Becuase for H2s there must the light go through this foil, and this foil is not optical clear.

Even if you get it on the glass without any bubbles, the H2s are slightly distorted.

posts.topic_title: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Dry mounting film to glass plates
posts.content_md:
> **andy75180:** I'm having trouble peeling off the protective layer ready for sticking the holographic film down. It took me 15 minutes to seperate it with a razor blade!!! What method do you use?

I just use my thumb nail. At times I have to snip off just the tip of the corner but most of the time I can just slip my fingernail underneath the cover sheet (as long as I don't cut my nails *too* short).

It's the sort of thing that comes with practice. There may be an easier way to do this but I haven't heard what it is.
